subsubtopic: SUGGESTED FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE FOR HOME OWNERS- MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I rise on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity under the provisions of Standing Order 43. The minister responsible for housing offered to intervene personally to assist Canadians faced with losing their homes due to excessively high interest rates. I have received, and I am still receiving, calls and letters asking for help from constituents in just such a predicament. Details of each case are being forwarded to the minister for prompt action by him. In light of the fact that these pleas for assistance are urgent and real in nature and they undoubtedly represent only a small percentage of home owners in serious trouble, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Prince Edward-Hastings (Mr. Ellis):
That the minister, hearing through Members of Parliament from Canadians in dire straits, now acknowledge the gravity and magnitude of the situation and pressure his government to stop passing the buck to the banks, accept its responsibility, and prepare an immediate plan of financial assistance for home owners.

The Minister of
State, when parliamentary secretary to the President of the Treasury Board, stated as follows:
-the government anticipates that its provisions will be made known in late November-

That this House urge the government to announce the date in November when it will make good on its moral responsibility for the victims of urea formaldehyde foam insulation.

S O. 43 VIA RAIL CALL FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF SPECIAL PARLIAMENTARY COMMITTEE-MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I wish to move a motion under the provisions of Standing Order 43. I rise on behalf of the hundreds of thousands of Canadians who have expressed their absolute opposition and dismay to the elimination of one fifth of Canada's rail passenger service, and to the callous way the government moved unilaterally to dismantle VIA Rail's transportation service. In view of the government's refusal to grant the people of Canada the right to be heard on this most important matter, and given the lack of clear and definitive policy on rail passenger service, I move, seconded by the right hon. member for Yellowhead (Mr. Clark):
That this House instruct the minister to rescind the order in council, and that a special select parliamentary committee be struck to hold full public hearings and to establish thoroughly a clear rail passenger policy and a clear VIA mandate so it can function on a sound financial and legal basis.
In support of this motion, I hereby submit for immediate consideration to the Prime Minister and to the Minister of Transport, the findings of a special Progressive Conservative task force on rail passenger service, entitled "The Last Straw", which hopefully all members will agree to have appended to Hansard of this date.

subsubtopic: FIGURES RELATING TO STARTS
speechtext: Madam Speaker, I wish to direct my question to the minister responsible for housing. At that trend, we are heading toward approximately 135,000 starts for the year, which represents a shortfall of 85,000. I might add that this confirms the predictions of the secret document which the minister has tried to disown. What advice does the minister have for Canadians who are now facing this critical housing shortage, which he finally recognizes as a housing crisis?

At the outset, I would like to say to him that I have been aware of changes and trends in the industry. I would indicate to him that on my last visit to his city, for example, I had the privilege of participating with the minister of housing for Newfoundland in the start of some social housing. In both those cases I think we have demonstrated that we are of assistance.

speakeroldname: Hon. James A. McGrath (St. John's East):
speechtext: Madam Speaker, I wish I could be gracious and return the compliment and congratulate the minister on his performance. Obviously I cannot do that because we are in a serious situation, largely as a result of the inability of the minister to respond to this crisis in the housing industry.
Hear, hear!

I wish to reflect the concern of many people in this country. The figures released by Statistics Canada yesterday indicate that there is a crisis. We are facing a zero vacancy rate by 1983 in the major markets of this country. Indeed, we have almost arrived at that point now.
According to his own document, this shortage will create a black market situation in which families will be forced to double up. It will bring on a Soviet Union kind of housing situation in this country.

Madam Speaker, in my first response I indicated that in starting this new term the government did a number of things to address the industry, which we recognized was facing difficulty and would face trend difficulties. For example, in his budget last
October 30, 1981

year the minister reintroduced capital cost provisions to assist on the supply side of housing through the MURB provision. That step taken by the government, which was abandoned by the government of which the hon. member was part, increased housing starts this year by an additional 20,000 units. speechtext: Madam Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Communications who will know that yesterday the government just lost its second case relating to the unauthorized reception of foreign signals from foreign satellites, with the result that the government's communications policy is left in tatters in that area. subsubtopic: RECEPTION OF TELEVISION SIGNALS VIA FOREIGN SATELLITES
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I would like to point out, first of all, that this is a prosecution which was not launched by the government, as such, but by the CRTC.
Obviously, it is a question of importance. While I am most sympathetic to the desires of the residents of Newfoundland to
receive PBS, as are many hundreds of thousands of Canadians, and I think we must find some way of seeing that they do receive this type of signal, the decision itself will undoubtedly be appealed, once we have had the opportunity of examining it because, if the initial reports that have come to me are correct, it has far-reaching implications.
The implication would be that any cable undertaking in this country could simply bring in whatever signals it wanted from American satellites and rebroadcast them over the Canadian system. That, in itself, may not be an unfortunate result, when one is looking at the PBS system, but there are a number of other signals on the American satellites, and the proliferation of such signals would endanger the continued existence of the Canadian broadcasting system as we know it. There are a number of other signals which are perhaps not as desirable as the PBS signals. I could mention the three pornographic channels that exist at the moment on American satellites.

speechtext:

subtopic: POSSIBILITY OF DISCUSSIONS WITH UNITED STATES
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, our interest, of course, is in seeing to it that all Canadians receive access to approximately the same number of signals no matter where they live in the country. The major initiative in that regard was taken last year when the CRTC authorized the CanCom organization, which is headquartered in Whitehorse, which is in the riding of the hon. member's House leader. That system itself is making available on satellite four television signals right across Canada-one from a Vancouver station, one from an Edmonton station, one from a Hamilton station, and another one which is basically a French language station-plus eight radio signals. Therefore, vast progress has been made in a very short period of time, making a larger number of signals available to Canadians in every part of the country.
On the question of extending what is commonly known as the three plus one rule, which is really the only subject of discussion at this moment, I do not believe that anyone in this House would want to argue that we should have a completely open sky policy in this country and that we should allow all Canadian cable companies, for instance, to rebroadcast every signal that is available off air or coming in from the United States satellites. On the question of three plus one, we have
October 30, 1981

already approached the American authorities and we have had discussions at the very preliminary state, and we will be continuing those discussions.

Mr. Speaker, in joining in this debate I think it would be wise to remind hon. members of what, in effect, Motions Nos. 21 and 22 would do if carried by the House as a suitable amendment to Bill C-48. The reason I say this is that I think often in debate in this House we get away from actually dealing with the motion before us.
If I may take a few minutes I would like to refer hon. members to Clause 27 of Bill C-48. This clause actually deals with what is called the Crown's share as anticipated by the government in what it calls the Canada lands. As the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Lalonde) has pointed out, Canada lands occupy approximately 40 per cent of the entire territory generally known as Canada, including offshore east coast, offshore west coast, the lands in the territories, the waters in areas such as the Hudson Bay and, of course, the Arctic and Beaufort Sea. It is a huge area. As we know, it is an area that is, in terms of the world's potential for oil and gas, if you like, one of the most attractive. There may be literally billions of barrels of oil and the equivalent of gas to be found in this area. The debate taking place today, especially as it relates to the Crown's share in those lands, is extremely important.
It is for this reason that I would first of all like to remind hon. members of the tremendous contrast between the effect of Motion No. 21, which is the motion of my colleague the hon. member for Etobicoke Centre (Mr. Wilson), and the bill itself. That hon. member, in effect, is saying that rather than have the federal government or the bureaucracy stepping in and arbitrarily taking 25 per cent of the Canada lands interests which a Canadian company-and I emphasize that-or a partly Canadian-owned company and partly foreign-owned company, or for that matter a foreign company, owns in these Canada lands, it would be better to change the measure to ensure that the only time the Crown can come in with a grab is when 50 per cent of the entire oil or gas play is not owned by Canadians.
In short, let me put three propositions. The first proposition would be when you had an entirely Canadian-owned company with not a share being owned by a foreigner. Let us assume, for example, that one of our pension funds owns the shares of the company. As the Crown proposes this clause, the clause which my colleague for Etobicoke Centre would like to amend, the Crown wants to grab a 25 per cent interest away from those Canadians. The Crown is, in effect, saying that, irrespective of the fact that the company is already 100 per cent Canadian owned, the bureaucracy, the federal treasury, wants to lift that 25 per cent interest out of the pockets of those pensioners whose funds hold the shares of that Canadian company. That is the one extreme.
The second proposition is when you have a company, let us say, such as Imperial Oil. Imperial Oil at the present time is
Canada Oil and Gas Act
approximately 70 per cent owned by its parent in the United States and almost 30 per cent Canadian owned. In that case, the government is saying that if Imperial Oil or Esso have certain interests in the Beaufort Sea or off the east coast, or on any of these Canada lands, it feels entitled to grab 25 per cent of what these companies have.
What my colleague from Etobicoke Centre is saying is that it is unfair. It is a retroactive grab. It is a grab that is not only unfair to the Canadian companies, as I hope members will agree, it is also unfair to companies such as Exxon which came to this country in good faith and developed those reserves, showed the potential that is there, only to find that 25 per cent of its interest is taken away without compensation. What my colleague is suggesting in Motion No. 21 is that it would be preferable for the Crown to simply say, in that case which I have cited, that it will take up to a 20 per cent interest, say, in what Imperial owns on the assumption that it is not willing to give up part of that 70 per cent block in Imperial Oil that it presently owns.
I suggest that if hon. members review what I am saying they will agree that is a fairer approach; it is more positive. In effect, it says to those who are now foreign concerns that we acknowledge they have brought these reserves into reality. They have demonstrated the potential of these reserves. These reserves are their assets but we are not going to steal those assets from them unless they fail to Canadianize to the extent of 51 per cent or more. If a company fails to make itself 50 per cent Canadian owned, we feel the Crown should be able to take over an interest which would be equal to whatever its deficiency is.
For example, in the case which I have cited, it would be a matter of saying to Imperial Oil that if it wants to retain that 70 per cent ownership, the Crown would be entitled to take up to 20 per cent of what it has. In turn, that will ensure that at least 50 per cent of the play is in Canada.
The other extreme, of course, is 100 per cent foreign ownership. If this company is 100 per cent foreign owned, it should be given the option to make itself 51 per cent Canadian owned, or if it does not wish to do that, it may be subject to a 25 per cent, or in our example even a 50 per cent, interest by the Crown itself. That is our party's position and I think it is a reasonable one. It is a position that is understandable and it is pro-Canadian as opposed to being anti-foreign. I believe this is a system which international investors would acknowledge as being not only equitable but fair. It is fair in the sense that these companies are not being confiscated without being given any option.

I believe we have before us in this bill a situation in which the government is proposing to steal property retroactively. It is nothing more than stealing. It is stealing property that has been won under the rules and regulations which the government saw fit to set for those who wished to participate in our oil and gas exploration and development. It is property that is owned by these concerns and is now proposed to be stolen retroactively by the government.
Some members of the government say they are now willing to give compensation for what it steals. I would refer the hon. members to the proceedings of the Standing Committee on National Resources and Public Works, issue No. 49 for Thursday, May 14, 1981, wherein the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources said with respect to this question of compensation:
The government then is fully satisfied that, as a balanced whole, the regime proposed in Bill C-48 is in every sense equitable.
Once a socialist says something like this, we know in his heart he realizes that it is not equitable. That is exactly what the minister goes on to explain. Having said it is equitable, he then says:
Nevertheless, to dispel any contrary concerns and arguments which may remain on the part of those who have been critical of the 25 per cent Crown
interest provision, we intend to provide reimbursement of actual exploration costs already incurred.
In this spirit of compromise then, we shall introduce amendments to provide for ex gratia payments in respect of 25 per cent of the geological, geophysical and drilling expenditures made up to December 31, 1980, in respect of any oil or gas discovery that results from a well spudded prior to that date and which qualifies to be declared a significant discovery prior to December 31, 1982. The qualifying expenditures will be determined on the same basis as those eligible for inclusion in the calculation set out for the progressive incremental royalty in Bill C-48.
These payments will be made out of the Crown share of production.
I notice that startles you, Mr. Speaker, because that is the ringer. The government is not going to pay the money upon seizure. It is going to say that if, as and when it gets something out of what it has taken, it will then give some of it back. The government says these payments will be made out of the Crown's share of production, that to reflect the value in time of qualifying expenditures, they will be escalated at the rate of 15 per cent a year up to December 31, 1980, and the government shall then pay 250 per cent of this escalated value of eligible expenditures as a first claim on the commercial production attributable to the 25 per cent Crown share. In short, what we have here is a partial payment being offered to those who will lose, say, 25 per cent of what they now own on Canada lands.
I emphasize once again that this may be conjured up by the government in the public sense as something that affects only foreign concerns. That is not true. Let us consider my example of a pension fund which has chosen-and some of them have- to invest in the oil and gas potential on our Canada lands. They will lose 25 per cent of workers' money invested to try to identify and bring resources into production, hopefully in some later year.
It is like some government official taking 25 per cent of the Canada Savings Bond a person has just bought. Let us say a person bought a $1,000 bond. What the government is doing is taking $250 of that. The person involved might say, "That is theft; I just bought it; how can you take it from me?" The government would say that the Parliament of Canada empowered it to do so. Then, feeling its neck a little the government would say, "Well, maybe we should give you something back". What does it do? It says that to the extent there are coupons payable to the government on the $250 it stole, the government will clip those coupons and give the person perhaps 5 per cent of what the government had already taken, without any compensation whatsoever. That is what the government is proposing.

Amendments should be proposed in the order of the lines of a clause. Mr. Speaker, I would first like to say that the speech by the hon. member for York-Peel (Mr. Stevens) indicates the deep con-

October 30, 1981
Canada Oil and Gas Act
cern that he, members of this House and people across this country have as a result of the government's proposed national energy policy. The policy creates more questions than it answers. In fact, I do not know what it answers. For a good many Canadians it will mean a much higher oil and gas bill with only negative results with regard to the objective all Canadians hoped for, energy self-sufficiency by 1990.
I speak as a maritime Member of Parliament. I wish to indicate a concern about my area of Canada. It is similar to that so ably expressed by the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Towers) about his part of Canada. What the hon. member for Carleton-Charlotte (Mr. McCain) expressed in this House yesterday about our part of Canada is also true for me.
It is absolutely essential that we strive to reach energy self-sufficiency by 1990 so that prospective developments can occur in Atlantic Canada. When we talk about the national energy policy and this bill which conceives it, we must realize that there can be no national energy policy until the federal government arrives at some type of positive agreement with the provinces of Nova Scotia and Newfoundland.
This bill will make it more difficult for Nova Scotia and Newfoundland to develop obvious energy possibilities off their coasts. I refer specifically to the Sable Island development off Nova Scotia, the Hibernia and other finds off the coast of Newfoundland. Before we can talk about any type of national energy policy, we must know that an arrangement has been made between the federal government and the governments of Nova Scotia and Newfoundland in relation to what will happen to those potential oil and gas developments.
We do not see anything positive happening. In his speech, the hon. member for Red Deer pointed out that the current casualty report shows that over 131 drilling rigs will leave this country this year, leaving behind 471 to do the type of drilling that is required if we are to hope for anything like energy self-sufficiency. Also, the development of the lands of western Canada, the Northwest Territories and the Yukon must be considered if we are to realize the energy self-sufficiency for which we all strive.
If Canada were a socialist country, and God knows no one would ever want that, there might be some possibility of this policy working. The government would have total control over the economy as is the case in Russia and Poland, if that is any recommendation these days. In this country the engine that drives the economy is the free enterprise system. It is only by working within that system that we can hope to achieve the elusive goal of energy self-sufficiency.
The approach of the Clark government was to harness the free enterprise system in such a way as to provide incentives to the oil and gas industry to develop our potential resources. The approach of the Clark government with regard to the east coast of Canada, the continental shelf, was to regard it as an extension of the resource development of the provinces where there was potential for oil and gas. If that had been followed through, the free enterprisers of Canada would now be moving into the energy sector in an attempt to find the resources that
are there. Rather than clarify the situation that exists, we have created complicated oil and gas regulations.
The government has said to those involved in the energy sector of this country: "We are an island unto ourselves." The reply to that has been: "We will go elsewhere to do our business in order that we can make a profit." The profit motive continues to be the driving force behind the free enterprise system. It is that force which keeps business here or sends it elsewhere. Today it is going elsewhere.
The reason there is absolutely no hope of ever attaining energy self-sufficiency in this country by 1990 is because of what this government is doing to Canadians in the oil and gas industry, not to the bogey-man or the multinationals, but to the individual Canadian who is the backbone of the oil and gas industry in Canada. What we are saying to him is: "You will have to make a decision to leave your country if you want to make any profit. If you stay here, we can almost guarantee that you will have to close your doors or go bankrupt if this policy goes into effect." That is what we are saying with this kind of legislation.
Some of the people involved in the oil and gas industry of Canada came down here to try and talk with politicians. They were not big fellows; they were not multimillionaires. They were fellows with trailer-truck operations and things like that. They were people who are necessary for the oil industry to remain healthy. They told me: "Unless this government does something that is positive, that reflects the free enterprise spirit that has built the oil industry in western Canada, we are finished; we will have to go to the United States or somewhere else."
That is not the kind of decision which means they can pick up their things and go to the United States today, returning in six months from now when the government realizes what it is doing to the industry and then trying to put their operation back together again. For instance, when 131 drilling rigs leave this country, do not expect them to come back next week or next month unless we change the legislation that is now before us. There is no way. Their commitment has to be for five years. No matter what we do with his package next week, next month or next year, once that decision to leave has been made, they are gone. We are then in deep trouble, as we are right now, and it is obvious.
I go back to the general election of February, 1980, to the period between December and January. I think of the debates that took place at that time, and I recall the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), who was then leader of the opposition, telling Canadians what a terrible thing the Clark budget would do to them. Mr. Speaker, if only they were given the opportunity today of returning to the Clark budget they would elect every member of the Progressive Conservative Party that supported that budget. There are no two ways about that. It was the best deal Canadians were ever offered. Unfortunately, Canadians were so mesmerized by the false advertising, the big lie, that they believed that they were going to be ripped off. The rip-off
October 30, 1981

started as soon as this government was elected and it continues. It is happening now, it will be happening tomorrow, it will be happening the next day. At the time of that election, it cost me and every other Canadian something like $18 to fill the gas tank of their car. It costs $28 today. By the time this government sees the people of Canada again, it will cost something like $75 to fill that same gas tank.
I go back to the people I really feel sorry for, people who will not drive their cars and who will turn to alternate forms of energy, if the Minister of Transport does not destroy all other forms of transportation. He is certainly taking rail transportation away from most Canadians as an energy efficient alternative to highway transport. But what will happen to the poor individual who has to heat his or her home? With the Clark government, there was built-in protection for those people as far as heating oil is concerned.
With this policy, this government will see a great many individual Canadians freeze in the dark. There will be no alternative for them but to freeze in the dark when you look at the escalation of heating costs already. We are not Florida. Regardless where people in this country live, they have to heat their homes nine months of the year. At this moment in time, most Canadians depend upon oil to do that heating. As far as heating oil prices are concerned, it is a terrible atrocity that has been afflicted on individual Canadians. There is no concern shown them. There is no built-in protection for the individual Canadian, especially for the one that requires assistance the most. I am not talking about the person on welfare. I am talking about the person who is not on welfare and who lives a lifetime saving, with none of our system geared to assist him, the Canadian who tries to maintain himself in dignity on a fixed income, but who discovers what a terrible atrocity is being visited upon him and others like him by this government with its so-called national energy policy.
I feel sorry for them because there is no chance at the moment for them to get back at this government and to teach them, as they can with their vote at the ballot box, what the electorate do to people who promote and propagate the big lie. Unfortunately, they will have to suffer. As members of this House, we should do everything we possibly can to assist them and to give them whatever protection is possible.
I say to my colleagues here, regardless of party, that if this institution is going to be responsible to individual Canadians, we will have to show them that we are concerned about the terrible commitment that this government is trying to make in its special deal against them. We have to see to it that this matter is rectified. We have to see that at least that part of the Crosbie budget that provided the individual, low-income Canadian with some special protection with regard to home heating fuel is put in place.
Prince Edward Island is totally dependent upon oil for the production of energy for all the people who live there. We have to provide some cushioning against these escalating increases of oil costs similar to what the Clark government again was negotiating with the Atlantic provinces. This is to protect a province like Prince Edward Island that is totally dependent

There are oil wells in the constituency of Assiniboia, most of which are low production wells. When we were defeated two years ago the situation in energy was that the consumer was paying approximately $1 per gallon for gasoline. The last two weeks have been very interesting and in some ways very entertaining. My hon. friends to the extreme right have to be commended. Over the last two weeks they have really done a splendid job. They have carried out an act that I did not think could be sustained like that for two solid weeks. Without even cracking a smile, hon. members have stood in their places, waved their arms, pointed their fingers and almost cried, complaining about socialism. I must say they have done a beautiful job of it. They have talked about blood on Liberals' sleeves and about the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) being a crypto-socialist. They have talked about confiscation and about robbery. To keep all of that going for two weeks without even cracking a smile, they deserve some kind of an actor's award. They have done so well that I might have believed them.
I am a socialist, of course. I might have taken some heart that this bill was socialist and believed them until I looked at some of the provisions in Bill C-48. Among other things I find that we will be giving 93 cents of every dollar to Canadian oil companies to spend on development. Oil companies get the 93 cents whether they find oil or not. If they find oil, however, and only if they find oil, the government takes back 35 cents, comprised of 25 cents in equity and ten cents in royalty. This 93 cents comes from the taxes of bus drivers, women who clean buildings, factory workers and all the other people who cannot dodge income taxes.
My leader asked the Prime Minister in the last few days about people who earn, say, $50,000 or $100,000 who can dodge paying their taxes, but his questions were brushed off. The money for oil exploration comes from people who cannot dodge their taxes, basically the wage or salary earner in Canada, the ordinary working man. Those are the people being taxed to give Canadian oil companies 93 cents of every dollar that they invest. If we are lucky, the country will get back 35 cents out of the 93 cents. If the working people are lucky, they may get some of that money back in education and health care.
These poor, starving oil companies are getting a free gift of only 58 cents out of every dollar spent on projects which will net them unlimited profits as the years go by and oil shortages increase. This is a subsidy oil companies are receiving from the bus drivers and other people who cannot dodge income tax. Hon. members to the right call it socialism. speechtext:
Motion No. 21 provides a logical solution to this expropriation act.
I am used to expropriation. The Minister of Transport (Mr. Pepin) knows why I am used to it. The Department of Transport took away 18,000 acres from people and then taxed them for that right. I think the minister could express a view on that. I think the minister knows the government goofed. He was not there, so he can duck out.
We are discussing a geographical area representing 40 per cent of the area of Canada. An area that size cannot be treated lightly. How are we treating the original citizens of this country? Are we looking after those citizens through this bill? We are expropriating their rights. We are taking away the rights of the original citizens. That is serious. Even under the provisions of Motion No. 22 it is not 25 per cent the government wants to take, but 50 per cent. These percentages are being taken away from the aboriginal people of the country. The rights of the few who are left in the territory will be taken away.

subsubtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING OIL AND GAS INTERESTS
speechtext: Whose rights?

subsubtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING OIL AND GAS INTERESTS
speechtext: You know whose rights.

subsubtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING OIL AND GAS INTERESTS
speechtext: Not native rights.

subsubtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING OIL AND GAS INTERESTS
speechtext:
This act does nothing more than give this government the right to expropriate on behalf of another Crown corporation. Like all Crown corporations, it will end up in the red, losing money and wasting the funds on itself rather than spending them for the good of Canadians. This bill does not help Canadian corporations, nor does it help anybody in the country. Even with this 25 per cent donation which the territories are giving to these people, a proper rate of return will not be provided compared to a rate of return which would be provided by the private sector. I would like to know what right the government has to expropriate the property of Canadian-controlled corporations. This is nothing more than a retroactive tax on Canadian citizens.
This bill also affects pension funds. Pension funds are involved in investment in energy in Canada and the amount of investment is large. Admittedly, while pension funds are being built up they are not taxed. They are exempt from tax. This is a hidden 25 per cent tax which will be imposed on pension funds in this country.
I think it is an absolute disgrace that our senior citizens have problems. We will have far greater problems when those born during the time of the last baby boom become senior citizens. Who will have to pay the bills? The bills better be paid by the private sector because the government is running out of money.
I ask this government to reconsider carefully our motion. There should be no expropriation of any corporation that is 51 per cent or more Canadian owned. Nor should there be any expropriation of a foreign corporation which makes an agreement to become Canadianized, that is 51 per cent owned by Canadians, through pension funds or investment by Canadian citizens.
Consider the shareholders in the pension fund of Imperial Oil, for example. Thirty per cent of Imperial Oil is owned by Canadians either through pension funds or money of individual citizens. While that is not a large amount, these people are being taxed through expropriation under Bill C-48. Will this government please consider this motion and look at it in light of what it is doing to Canadian citizens? It is inequitable and unfair.
My colleague the hon. member for York-Peel (Mr. Stevens) stated earlier that if there is only 30 per cent of Imperial Oil that is Canadian owned, then take 20 per cent; but work out some arrangement which will encourage foreign corporations to Canadianize, rather than a method that is blatantly dictatorial. This cannot all be done in one fell swoop; it must be worked through over a period of time.
Free enterprise with foreign capital debt will assist this country to develop our oil. The Canadian government has run out of credit. It has run out of dollars, and its great friend, Dome, has also run out of money. It is now sitting on the edge of the fence praying to God that oil is found in one of the three
October 30, 1981

or four holes or however many it drilled this summer, in order to relieve some of its financial woes.
What we are not looking at in this bill, and what we have not appreciated in this entire National Energy Program discussion, is the small Canadian producer. We have not considered the service contractors. It is time this government started paying attention to the majority of Canadians, the little guy who makes his living from small business. How will this government hurt these people? Perhaps in one respect it has done them a favour. The government has forced them to go into the United States; it has forced them out of Canada. What is that doing for Canada? It is driving our funds away, driving our money out of this country and creating an imbalance in capital flow. By following this entire National Energy Program, as exemplified by Bill C-48, we are hurting the Canadian citizen.
The climate is entirely wrong in Canada today with this present government's policies. Will the government please change the legislation in order to attract the Canadian entrepreneur who wants to stay in this country, who wants to succeed and to benefit from our great riches? All we are doing is driving this country into what the government calls Canadi-anization, what I call nationalization or socialism, or, to go one step further, communism, where the state owns everything. This is all being done by degrees. Hon. members can make all the noise they want but they will not change the situation or the dangerous route we are following.
Do you realize, Mr. Speaker that this measure permits the government to commit a criminal act, namely, straight, direct robbery. The citizens who elected this government would go to jail if they followed this practice. This government is above it all. It can do whatever it wants. The government laughs at these people. I hear hon. members laughing at them every day. The Minister of Transport laughs at them because he is taking their transportation away. The Minister of Communications (Mr. Fox) laughs at them. He is taking away their opportunity to listen to good programs from all over the world. Perhaps I should take that back as I understand he is relenting on his original stand.
I have been involved in the private sector all my life. I have done something that many people in this chamber have never done, namely, I have met payrolls. That is difficult to do when you are a small-business man starting up in this country. But there is an opportunity to meet payrolls in this country and there is an opportunity for people like ourselves to create industry here. Why is this government so dedicated to stopping that? Hon. member should just go out and try to raise capital in Canada for a small oil company. First of all, your foreign markets are cut off. Secondly, interest rates are so high we cannot afford to borrow money from the banks.
The government has eliminated opportunity for Canadians, and that is why I am angry. I am damned annoyed at what this government is doing to the citizens of this country. It should be making it easier for them to raise funds wherever they can in order to create labour wherever that is possible. The government should not be destroying incentive for the
Canada Oil and Gas Act
entrepreneur. I know how damned hard it is to raise money, but today it is impossible for small oil companies to do so.
What is happening? Small oil companies have only one route to follow; they are being taken over by the larger companies, and one reads about that every week in the newspaper. The government is eliminating the little guy. In this country you have to be a multi-multi-millionaire to exist. The little guy does not have a hope. The entrepreneur is prepared to give up something in order to create labour. I believe it is now time for this government to be prepared to give up something in order to create labour and solve some of the problems in Canada.
This bill with this 25 per cent hidden tax removes any real incentive there is left for Canadians to invest in Canada or to raise foreign capital. My recommendation to the people is that as long as there is the hostility in the atmosphere created by this administration, they should not invest in Canada. I have talked to many people over many days about a great deal of things, but one question keeps coming up; why bother investing in Canada with the rate of return that has been created by this government? This government is taking over two thirds of the revenue received from every barrel of oil. It thinks it is going to attain energy self-sufficiency. This government is on its knees praying to God that somebody will hit enough oil in some of these expropriated lands that we will have enough oil to look after us in 1990. I assure you, Mr. Speaker, that it will have to do more than pray, because it takes a lot of money to achieve that. It takes more than prayer to accomplish things in this world; it takes hard work. You have to get your hands dirty and your brow must sweat.
I do not see any point in investing in Canada. I think it is a tragic thing for me to have to stand in this chamber and say that. I think it is tragic that we are at the point where there is such a hostile atmosphere that it is not wise for Canadians to stay here.
The one benefit which will come out of the National Energy Program is that American and foreign banks are flooding into Canada because of our fantastic interest rates. They are all getting charters. I am not against this; I am merely pointing out that this is the only group which will benefit from the National Energy Program. I believe in competition, Mr. Speaker, but the foreign banks will benefit because no Canadians will invest. People who are investing are the ones with depth, going into the company paying a 20 per cent return. But that money is flowing straight out of the country again. They definitely will be beneficiaries. Many of these banks are coming into Canada for that reason alone. Their head offices may be on Bay Street in Toronto, but the administrative offices are in Calgary where the action is.
How long can small companies continue to borrow at these rates and still exist? There is no future for investment in this country. The government should be thinking of trying to attract funds which have gone out of this country back to Canada where they should be invested.

October 30, 1981
Canada Oil and Gas Act
I know the Liberal government will not listen to us on Motion 21. I am fully aware that they will do nothing about it and will just bulldoze it through, as they do everything else. But I plead with them to be considerate. They are imposing a tax on Canadian citizens and on pension funds throughout this country.
I would like to reiterate that the territories we are concerned with are hopeful of becoming provinces one day. This act automatically treats them as have-not provinces. The federal government, which wants to take a quarter of their money away from them, and the socialists to my left who want to take 50 per cent, will be creating have-not provinces. Before this bill is passed we should consider the territories and the poverty they will suffer under this bill even before they become provinces.
I am concerned that this country grow, particularly in the north. If these territories are turned into poverty areas before they are even permitted access to provincial rights, no one will be attracted to that region. This bill will remove their future provincial rights and the rights of the original settlers of that part of the country.

subsubtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING OIL AND GAS INTERESTS

Look at the negative effects on the economy of Canada and at the shrinkage in manufacturing resulting from the National Energy Program and Bill C-48. These measures, along with the exorbitant spending of this government over the last 15 years, have resulted in shrinking the manufacturing facilities of this country, as well as the processing and contracting facilities, including housing.
The Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) during the previous election campaign made the statement that if any injury or significant disadvantage is experienced by any group, he would remove the burden in the subsequent budget. I hope he remembers his own words when he considers the next budget. This bill, Mr. Speaker, does nothing more than compound the inflation spiral by siphoning off this money to a Crown corporation which does not give the same benefit to a Canadian citizen. All it does is increase the price of fuel oil, gas and heating oil. Under this bill there are absolutely no benefits received by the citizens of this country.

Speaker was one of the class of '72. I understand my friend, the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pepin), went the other way in 1972, and I have the impression that sometimes he wishes it was 1972 again.

subsubtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING OIL AND GAS INTERESTS

speechtext:
That was the election where we lost by two seats. It could have been one of the best governments we ever had, under Mr. Stanfield.
I would also like to mention that the maiden speech given by the hon. member for Spadina (Mr. Heap) indicates a person is let off scot free during a maiden speech, but only one time. I noticed that he tried to have it and keep it too, but I did enjoy his speech. I very much favour short sermons.
I would like to speak today on Motion No. 21 put forward by our party, and Motion No. 22 put forward by the New Democratic Party. The hon. member from Vancouver-Kings-way (Mr. Waddell) is very quick to claim credit for taking away the Mackenzie Valley pipeline, but he is not so quick to take credit for causing the tankers to show up in the Strait of Juan de Fuca because there is no pipeline through which to send Alaskan oil. However, that is his problem, not ours. The NDP have a lot to say on this issue. They are suffering under the rather serious handicap of having western membership and eastern leadership.

subsubtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING OIL AND GAS INTERESTS
speechtext: You have the problem. You have western membership and no leadership.

subsubtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING OIL AND GAS INTERESTS
speechtext:
I can appreciate the extremes to which they go when they have to send missionaries from Etobicoke to run for seats in Vancouver.
I will now discuss Motion No. 21 and the difference it is going to make. This bill represents a rather serious incursion by the government into private industry. It is very serious indeed.
I would like to point out some of the problems we would have by an incursion of the government into not only the marketplace, or industry, but almost every aspect of Canadian life. With respect to investment, it is questionable whether this is really investment and we hope to stop this through Motion 21. It is borrowing the resource and paying for it some other time. I would not go so far as to say that the government is stealing from the industry, as some of my colleagues have stated. But they are taking it without the owner's permission.
I understand the speech of the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) the other day was headlined "Caring and Sharing . The government would rather the industry take care of the resources and the government share them. That is how we came to Bill C-48, so the government could get in on the sharing part. Although the government would like to share in the success, if the company loses money it will turn it back to the industry and give it 100 per cent of the losses.
I might point out some interesting figures which were released mainly by government agencies. The first one I would like to mention is the current gross fixed capital formation in
October 30, 1981

government investment, and it has gone down steadily since 1960 as a percentage of gross national expenditures. In 1960 it was 4.1 per cent; in 1965, 4.4 per cent; in 1970, 3.7 per cent; in
1975,	3.8 per cent; and in 1980, 2.8 per cent. That is a percentage of gross national expenditure, so that means excluding inflationary figures.
[DOT] (M50)
If we were using inflationary figures, we all realize it would be a sum of billions of dollars going steadily upward. However, when we look at that, we can see that government fixed capital formation is not working out any more than government funded research and development is, which is, interestingly enough, in the same schedule issued by the Department of Finance in April, 1981, showing that government funded research and development increased from 0.62 per cent to 0.65 per cent between 1960 and 1965 and since then went down in 1975 to 0.48 per cent and in 1980 to 0.46 per cent. Despite the great claims of various ministers, the research and development program has not been producing. It is getting to be more and more miserly.
What I am putting across is that the funds which are being expended by the government are more and more getting to have less and less to do with the future of the country. They are just current transfers of payments to individuals. They are not hooked to something that is really good for the country, such as investment in plant, in training or in research and development.
Trends in government employment are of some interest and, I believe, illustrate again the point I am making. The percentage of government employment as compared with total employment in 1961 was 22.1 per cent. That figure went steadily up each and every year since then until it is now 24.3 per cent. However, if we look at government wages as a percentage of total wages, we find a rather peculiar situation. In 1961 government wages as a percentage of total wages paid in this country were 19.4 per cent. In 1965 that figure was 19.7 per cent; in 1970, 23.1 per cent; in 1975, 24.3 per cent; in
1976,	24.9 per cent; and in 1977, 25.1 per cent. Hon. members will notice that while there has been very little increase in the number of people employed, there has been quite a substantial increase in the amount of money spent by the government in wages. This indicates simply that the fat cats are getting fatter and fatter as the years go by. I do not think this is really what the government or the people of Canada are looking for. This may be why surveys taken in Ottawa about mortgage problems come up almost blank. This is the fattest of all fat cities. I am glad to see that the hon. member for Ottawa Centre (Mr. Evans) is here to agree with me. I imagine he would. There are very few people in Ottawa who have financial difficulties. There are many people everywhere else who have.
It is clear that the government has tended in the past 20 years to decrease its spending on capital and on research- these are two types of activities which can be viewed as akin to investments-and to increase demand on the economy's available work force. Moreover, the work force which the govern-
Canada Oil and Gas Act
ment is employing has become more expensive, whether because of higher salaries for similar work or through alterations in the type of work performed for government. The change is clearly one away from investment and toward increasing current consumption.
I would like to talk for some time about federalism, the fiscal arrangements we have and energy taxes. After all, is that not what the motion is all about?
There are two events-one is now in process; that is, this event, and the other has just concluded-which are going to alter substantially the fiscal structure of the Canadian confederation. The first of these events was the settlement between Ottawa and the oil producing provinces of their disputes over the production and pricing of oil and gas. The second is the current renegotiation of intergovernmental transfer programs and specifically discussions about the amendments to federal-provincial arrangements and the Established Programs Financing Act. As the recent energy pricing disputes are best understood in the context of fiscal renegotiations, I will talk about them first.
Fiscal renegotiations between levels of government are not normally the cause of great strains within a country. Even less frequently do they penetrate the public consciousness. In Canada, however, they have become, and will be for at least the next five years, a focus of a great deal of the constitutional debate. Please let us not think that the constitutional debate will end Monday, Tuesday or Wednesday. There will be years of debate on the Constitution, no matter what the results are on Monday, Tuesday and Wednesday next. The details of the settlement which will come about after the renegotiation of the fiscal arrangements will affect not just the economic structure of the country, and particularly its tax structure. In addition, the negotiations and the process whereby a resolution is achieved will themselves profoundly affect the politics of this country. In essence the federal government is embarking upon a course which will almost inevitably bring it into serious conflict with a number of provinces. Given the current strains on confederation and the existence of a government in Quebec which wants, at the least, a dramatic restructuring of the country-and, indeed, Quebec was promised that by those occupying the government benches during the recent referendum campaign in Quebec-there is clear potential for a major crisis which will be fought over this issue.
With its very large deficit the federal government faces a serious dilemma. It has very large obligations stemming directly from the regional equalization role it performs as well as from related regional transfers. At the same time the government is unwilling to raise visible taxes to any degree. This is no doubt hampering the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) a great deal. In several election campaigns the government has built up the expectation that it will never raise taxes. It simply imposes taxes in a way that is invisible. We do not pay a high price for gasoline because gasoline is more expensive; we do so becasue there is a much higher tax component. Every gallon is taxed far more than it was two years ago.

October 30, 1981
Canada Oil and Gas Act
As the federal government views the problem, its crux lies in the fact that Ottawa has responsibility for alleviating regional disparities which have been made more extreme, in large part because of the explosion of the value of the west's resource riches while having relatively little access to the additional revenues generated. In short, the central government wants a drastic rearrangement of fiscal priorities to facilitate the current level of transfers from richer to poorer provinces without bankrupting the federal government, and to ensure that Ottawa's visibility as a provider of services is as great as its visibility as a collector of taxes. This is a problem any government faces. Everybody wants to be Santa Claus, and up until the present time the government has been able to perform that role because of the increases which sprang, for a time, from the inflation which was rampant and has been rampant for the last 12 years in this country. However, for a time it expanded the tax take of the government quite considerably and naturally. Then indexation of taxation took place; this restricted the amount the federal government stood to gain from inflation, and immediately it began to get into fiscal trouble. The federal government had by then developed the idea that it need never raise taxes but could go on spending more and more money. With the indexation of taxation the government was unable to do so. I thought that its only alternative was.to go into debt, so it proceeded to do that rather than face the problem honestly and try to move toward having our income and our outflow of funds equalized.
In two months it will be two years since the Crosbie budget did its best to put this country on a sensible economic path. It does not appear possible for the Liberals to do anything except run expenditures up with the taxpayer's dollar. They now have an additional bonanza in the energy agreement which will supply them with some $50 billion in the next few years. The government looks upon this as found money. Suddenly they have inherited this money and now, I expect, they will look for ways to spend it. We would prefer that they pay some attention to the Economic Council of Canada. Perhaps the council s statement in its recent paper on fiscal arrangements should be read into the record at this time. It reads:
-but the federal deficit problem cannot be solved by transferring the problem to the provinces. Not only do those economic trends indicate inadequacy of such an approach, but also council projections show that the coming decade will require investment at an unprecedented level in Canada, probably as high or higher than the peak periods of investment reached so far this century. This means that all governments will have not only to restrain their spending but also to raise taxes. Only then will they be able to encourage the financing of investment activities of the sort required. Given the difficulties with restraint, the different levels of government will want to shift the burdens of any increase in taxes to each other. The political ramifications of policies calling for increased taxes inevitably lead in this direction. But this exchange of burdens goes nowhere toward solving Canada's economic difficulties.
As these talks begin in the next few weeks, I would strongly recommend to the Minister of Finance that he remember that what one gets away with in one area is simply imposed in another. If they are going to squabble over the tax dollars, they must remember the pot is only a certain size and they have to share it. I have complained about the ever-increasing
government intervention in private industry and the problem of increasing labour costs of such intervention.
I would like to conclude with a quote from a famous analyst of bureaucracy, namely, Max Weber. He identified one characteristic of the bureaucracy early in this century in this way:
Bureaucratization offers above all the optimum possibility for carrying through the principle of specializing administrative functions according to purely objective considerations ... The "objective" discharge of business primarily means discharge of business according to calculable rules and "without regard for persons."
This has a danger. It is an attractive way to do things. The only problem is that it does not work very well. Nobody is ever to blame. The blame is shared. The bureaucracy assumes it as a whole. Things go on, Ottawa gets bigger and fatter, and the people pay more and more for less and less. I hope this motion will come to a vote fairly soon. I thank the House for its kind attention.

Motion No. 23
That Bill C-48, an act to regulate oil and gas interests in Canada lands and to amend the Oil and Gas Production and Conservation Act, be amended in Clause 28 by striking lines 13 to 17 at page 16 and substituting the following therefor:
"former lease under which significant or commercial discoveries of oil or gas were made on or before October 28, 1980 or in respect of any interest that succeeds that former lease".

subsubtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING OIL AND GAS INTERESTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, Motion No. 23 deals with the exemption of certain properties under the Canada Lands Act. Where production has occurred prior to December 31, 1980, these lands are to be exempted from the back-in provision. As everyone knows, the only production we have on Canada lands today is Norman Wells and the gas
October 30, 1981

production at Pointed Mountain. In effect there are two properties.
The position of the Conservative Party is that we do not believe in any form of confiscation. We do not think this back-in is right. What we are proposing in our motion is that at the very least those companies which have gone out in the Canada lands and have made a discovery of oil or gas should be exempted from that back-in provision. After all, they have spent money, gone out and proved up an asset. I think it is fair that anyone who has discovered oil or gas on Canada lands prior to December 31, 1980, should be exempt from this back-in provision. It is confiscation in any form, but it is that much more so in this case if a discovery has been made on the land. That is the intent of Motion No. 23.
When speaking on Bill C-48 the other day, I attempted to describe what self-sufficiency means in Canada, what we are looking at over the next 10 to 20 years, and the formidable job ahead of us if we are to approach even any kind of oil self-sufficiency in Canada. In my previous speech I said that Canada is looking at a shortfall of a million barrels of oil a day. I attempted to describe what an immense job it will be for Canada to try to find a million barrels of oil a day.
There is another aspect of Bill C-48 that I want to address this afternoon. In my view, the impact of Bill C-48 will have a devastating effect on many other aspects of economic life in our country. I am concerned that when we talk about Canadi-anization, and let us assume it is Canadianization and not nationalization-

I should like to return to what I believe to be the broader aspects of Bill C-48 and their impact on Canada. One question we should consider is where we will find the money. Energy self-sufficiency is a nice goal. It sounds nice, it is a nice phrase. But where will we find the money? Not only will we be required to find money to finance one million barrels of new oil production per day, but we will have to find money for a lot of other things in the next 20 to 30 to 50 years in Canada. Do we think we can get it all by ourselves? Can we generate all this cash by ourselves in Canada?
I was interested in a talk given the other day by Mr. Ed Neufeld, the senior vice-president and chief economist of the Royal Bank of Canada. The title of his talk was "Who will Finance Canada's Economic Growth in the 1980s?"

I am not sure whether hon. gentlemen on my left really care, but the Conservative Party cares about financing Canada's economic growth. It is important to us because it means jobs and incomes for Canadians. Mr. Neufeld said that we would need $1.4 trillion in the next decade to finance our growth. It is beyond my comprehension-$1.4 trillion. This is a staggering sum of money. The Canadian government spends $65 billion a year. What is that in terms of $1.4 trillion? Is it 20 or 200 times that amount?
Mr. Neufeld also said that of this $1.4 trillion, $300 billion will be required in energy and energy-related areas but that huge amounts will also be required in metal mining, pulp and paper, transportation, chemicals, the steel industry, and so on. He went on to say that the rapid development of investment in technology will be the single most important element for achieving Canada's productivity potential. Where will we get $1.4 trillion? I guess much of it depends on the ability of Canadian business to generate its capital requirements. Mr. Neufeld also said that business will have to raise $900 billion of this $1.4 trillion. What does this mean? It means that Canada must have a healthy private sector industry to generate that cash flow.
He went on to indicate that individual Canadians will have to put up $400 billion from their savings in the next 10 years. This means that Canadians should be able to save, to go out and to work. They should have adequate incomes. They cannot be taxed out of existence, or they will not have any money to save and reinvest in their own country.
He went on to say that the government will be required to put up $60 billion. We will need foreign investment, and we must recognize this. Business will have to put up $900 billion, so we need a strong entrepreneurial society to go out and create that cash flow. Individual Canadians need an opportunity to invest in Canada. They need the incomes and jobs to create that investment. We need foreign investment capital.
How will we encourage the foreign investment capital we desperately need when the legislation before us this afternoon is put into effect? Has the government thought about that? Does it care? I presume that it does not really care. We will not have any access to foreign capital. We will not get it. People will not invest in Canada. They do not want to invest in a country which will confiscate their assets. Would any hon. member invest in good faith in a country the government of which would come along and steal it?

The assets belong to the companies that invested in Canadian land. The government is not only expropriating the assets of foreigners, it is expropriating the assets of Canadian companies which have invested in Canada.
The Canadian ambassador went on to say that the Americans should be tolerant of the course Canada is pursuing through its energy policies. How tolerant would hon. members opposite be if somebody walked into their living rooms and stole their property? Would they be tolerant?
I wonder whether hon. members opposite understand how difficult it is to raise capital. How many of them have gone out to raise capital for a new plant? Minister of State for Mines (Mrs. Erola) ever try to raise capital to do anything worth while?

subsubtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING OIL AND GAS INTERESTS
speechtext:
Did she ever try to raise money to drill an oil well or to purchase a drilling rig? I have been there. I tried to raise capital for 20 years and it was darned difficult. I can remember making many trips to Toronto and Montreal in the 1950s, 1960s and 1970s trying to raise money for oil and gas development, for oil well drilling rigs and to expand the company. Not a dime could I raise because the banks and eastern Canadian investors thought the business was too risky. It is a lot easier to steal it than to go out and make it. The government and hon. members opposite know that. I had to go to Houston and Dallas to raise capital. I could not raise it in Canada, but I could raise it in Houston and Dallas because the people there saw the opportunity which existed in western Canada. It was too risky for Canadians.
The last company for which I worked started from nothing. It started with one rig in Estevan, Saskatchewan. The rig cost $125,000 in 1964. The company started with 15 employees. In a period of 15 years the company managed to survive through some good times and bad. It grew, and it grew on foreign capital. It did not grow on Canadian capital; it grew on foreign capital. The company was sold in 1979 to another Canadian company. At that time, it had become the largest land-based oil well drilling and servicing contractor in North America. It employed over 1,500 people, of whom 1,000 were Canadians. It is U.S. capital that made it possible. It created 1,000 jobs in Canada and 500 jobs in the United States. The company drilled a couple of thousand wells over a period of 15 years and made a positive contribution to the ecomomic wealth of Canada, but it also made a positive contribution to the
welfare of 1,000 Canadian workers. Many of those employees owned shares in the company and they took pride in that ownership.
If I were to make a single point with regard to the success of that company, it would be that the employees who owned shares, who owned a piece of that company, took great pride in the achievements and the success of that company. I cannot tell you how many of those employees valued and respected their ownership in that company.
There is a right way and a wrong way to Canadianize Canadian industry. The right way is to allow Canadians and Canadian employees to acquire shares in Canadian companies. The wrong way is for the government to do it for them. How can you create incentive and pride among employees when the government owns the asset? Answer that question. Would you take any personal pride in your home if the government owned it? Would you take any personal pride in your automobile if the government owned it? There is the difference between state ownership and individual ownership.
Hon. members opposite seem to forget that vital point. It is pride that makes people go out and work in this life. It is not a kick-in-the-ass type of philosophy that is exploited by the Liberal government.
Canada needs large amounts of foreign investment in years to come. When we talk about foreign investment, we talk about real jobs for real, live, Canadians. We talk about incomes for Canadian people. Surely that is the direction in which government policy should go.
It seems crazy to me that we should deny Canadians the opportunity to invest in their own country and that we should discourage foreign investment capital that we need in Canada to create a healthy productive economy.
How much capital is required to create one job in Canada? Does anyone know? It varies from industry to industry. I think $100,000 per job is probably a very low estimate.
I see the hon. member for Ottawa-Centre (Mr. Evans) shaking his head and saying that it does not cost $100,000 to create a job in Canada. I have looked at a number of figures and I believe it is a very conservative number. In any event, it is $100,000 a job. How many jobs do we need to create in Canada in the next ten years? One million? I am pointing out to you that the amounts of money that will be required to create the investment for a healthy and productive economy for this country are staggering. We cannot do this all ourselves and fulfil the aspirations of the Canadian people. We will have to rely on foreign investment capital, whether we like it or not. Canada with 23 or 24 million people, cannot live as a nation unto itself. It is beyond our financial resources. What do we do? Do we constrain ourselves and our productive capacity and contrain the aspirations of Canadians? Do we do this because we simply want to go out and raise capital to do something? What is wrong? Tell me, what is the difference between capital from Belgium and capital out of your pocket?
October 30, 1981

Does it have a different colour to it? Do you pay a different rate of interest on the money?
We have our own federal government that borrows money on foreign markets. It is all right for the federal government to borrow those funds, but it is not all right for the private business to do it. That is bad. I do not understand the logic of that.
We are playing a very dangerous game with our friends in the world in terms of foreign investment. We have not only turned off the United States, but we have turned off the Germans, the Dutch and the British. I have been there and I have listened to them. They do not want to have anything to do with Canada any more. They do not want us. They do not even trade with us. As far as they are concerned, we have failed to live up to our international obligations under the GATT agreement and they will take us to court. That is how they feel about us. I do not care whether the Canadian ambassador says, "Be tolerant and respect our policies," because it will not drill and it will not sell. They are not buying. The Canadian government will not pay the price but individual Canadians will pay it. It is not you. You will not suffer, and I will not suffer. However, individual Canadians will suffer because of this policy. You can bet on it.
It is not as though Canada were the only country in the world that needs capital investment. Do we really believe that we are all that great and that we are the only country in the world that needs capital investment today? Others should consider it a privilege to lend us money to develop our economy. Every country in the world needs capital investment, and lots of it.

made could have a significant and profound effect on the wellbeing of Canada.
A great many western Canadian members have taken part in this debate. Some say that the development of high technology in eastern Canada is the business only of eastern Canadians and that somehow or other the development of the resources in western Canada is the business only of western Canadians. Both of these statements are, of course, untrue. We are intertwined in this country by every advance and every backward step that is taken in developing any part of Canada. If a backward step is taken in the forest industry in British Columbia, it ripples across the nation. If an advance is made in the resource industries in western Canada, we are all affected by it. All Canadians have a vital interest in the continued and growing vitality of the nation.
From time to time we tend to think of these debates in regional terms. They have a direct impact on the regions affected, but ripples cut across boundaries, waves wash over boundaries, and it does not matter.
If a step is taken by any government advancing any good principle-and Canadianization is a good principle-people from every part of Canada are involved. However, if a step is taken that has a deleterious effect on one of our major industries, particularly one in which there is some capability for growth, then people from every part of Canada have to become concerned. Therefore, I think it is relevant to the people in my constituency and in my part of Canada, just as it is relevant to my friends in the province of Quebec, to be very much concerned, just as an increasing number of knowledgeable economic writers and commentators are concerned about the effect of the National Energy Program on the resource industry in western Canada.
This is not a concern reflected just in partisan terms about government policy toward the development of business in Canada. The same concern was reflected the other day in a statement made by Mr. Thomas Kierans who is the retiring chairman of the Ontario Economic Council. Mr. W. A. Macdonald, a distinguished Toronto lawyer and member of the McMillan Binch firm spoke in similar terms. I am sure hon. members recognize the McMillan Binch firm as the firm John Turner went to. We should stop and take stock of where we are moving. If we are moving in the right direction, are we using the right tools and are we on the right track? Are we going too quickly? Is the speed at which we are travelling having deleterious effects?
I am sure all those who heard the special report carried by the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation broadcast in the early part of this week must have been moved by the discussions on activities in western Canada. When I was in Regina, Edmonton and Vancouver, I talked to a great many people, not just Conservatives but people who are interested in the development of Canada as much as anyone else is. Since the National Energy Program began, more than 100 drilling rigs have left the country. If my figures are incorrect and they can be checked, I will certainly correct them on the record. But the movement of 100 rigs is a major movement. Drilling rigs are not like hand pumps that one can pull out of the ground, they are not like electric drills that can be moved easily. The movement of one drilling rig involves 30 trucks. A big decision is made when a rig is moved. Where are these drilling rigs going? They are not going to the United States because their owners like Americans more than they like Canadians. It is not that at all. I do not believe rigs are leaving Canada because their owners do not like the policies of the government of Alberta. They may not, but I do not believe that is the reason. If anyone can tell me of a commentator who would say that, I would like to know. Drilling rigs are being moved by their owners because of the National Energy Program. People are concerned about the Canadianization policy. They are concerned about the the proposals involving Canada lands. Given that kind of concern, it is only natural people turn to the United States.
I am not suggesting at all by what I am saying that companies should have an untrammelled right with respect to Canada lands, but I think we have to stop, look and listen to what has happened. We must listen to those who are knowledgeable in the business. We must ask ourselves whether the policy, of which this bill is the keystone, is really in the best interests of the country, given the speed of implementation and given the side effects from it. That is of interest to us because I believe it can be demonstrated that for every Canadian job lost in Alberta, for every drilling rig which is taken out of Canada, and for every negative shift, the impact is not felt only in Drayton, Alberta; it is felt in Ontario among the suppliers of valves, pipes, fittings, trucks, drills and all of the things manufactured here and used in the drilling industry. This can have an impact on the petrochemical industry in Sarnia, represented by my friend, the hon. member for Sarnia (Mr. Cullen) who is in the House. We are not little islands in this country, we are joined together as one country in the economic sense, and that is the course of the matter. That is the thing that concerns and worries me about this bill.
I had determined not to enter the debate until I heard my friend, the hon. member for Calgary South. I think it is very important that the government not consider anyone who is opposed to the bill as being opposed to Canadianization, but that at least it consider another way to Canadianize. 1 hope it is considering other ways.
I do not have to tell you, Mr. Speaker, about the importance of foreign capital to the industry. My friends have talked about that importance, and it is important. You represent a part of the province of Ontario, as I do, and you must know, as I know, the concerns there are within the province of Ontario regarding the whole question of deindustrialization. We do not have oil here. We have some very small quantities of natural gas, but we do not have oil. If we are to see our growth, it will be in high technology, in the developing, manufacturing,
assembling and processing industries. That is not happening in Ontario at the moment. That is one of the difficulties of this province. If we are to have balanced economic growth, I believe it is important to have growth everywhere.
One of the things that you and I encountered, Mr. Speaker, when we were in the Republic of Germany was that wherever we went-and you will recall that we met Chancellor Helmut Schmidt, provincial officials in Stuttgart and officials in Bonn, we met them socially, as you will recall, and we also met them at the session of the committees of the parliament in Bonn- was their puzzlement, they were scratching their heads. They wondered why we took this kind of universal approach to the question of foreign capital. They indicted a willingness to enter into joint ventures with us, ventures in which they did not want the majority holding. They are interested in making money and they look upon Canada, they thought, as a reasonable place in which to invest, but they scratched their heads. I think this government too is beginning to scratch its head a little about this matter.
As the hon. member for Calgary South has said, jobs are created as a result of the creation, the building, the augmenting of industry in any part of Canada. There is a great problem in Canada with respect to jobs. We have a million Canadians unemployed. We have people who are trained to do some jobs, but there is no place for them to work. We have people who are educated but because there is no development at the moment, they find themselves underemployed. There is nothing wrong with working at what might be termed a job at an ordinary level, but it is a shame if a person is trained to work at something different and cannot do it. That is a concern we all must have, and I gather the government is suddenly becoming concerned about it.
All those brave words in the Speech from the Throne have come to nothing. Little has been heard recently of the Foreign Investment Review Agency, and little has been heard about the strengthening of it. The reason is that it was regarded, and is becoming , regarded within the Liberal government, I think, as a matter that will slow the pace of needed development. The same can apply to any government policy. However we like to cut it, in the resource industry in western Canada at the moment the application and the pace of the program under the national energy policy as announced, and the form and method of Canadianization, is having that kind of dulling effect on the cutting edge of one of our industries with the greatest potential in Canada.
